questions.stem: How does Hamlet begin?
options: Fortinbras and his army arrive at the gates of Elsinore in the night
Guards on the battlements of Elsinore see the ghost of the dead King
Hamlet returns from Wittenberg to find his mother already remarried
Claudius is crowned king in a public ceremony in front of the court
questions.explanation: The play opens at midnight with nervous sentries asking 'Who's there?' The Ghost of old King Hamlet appears to them and to Horatio, and they decide to tell young Hamlet.

questions.stem: What has happened in Denmark just before the play begins?
options: King Hamlet has been killed in battle by Fortinbras, who now threatens to invade
King Hamlet has died, and Prince Hamlet has been crowned but is thought too young to rule
King Hamlet has died, and Gertrude now rules Denmark as regent for her son
King Hamlet has died, and his brother Claudius has become king and married Gertrude
questions.explanation: Within weeks of old Hamlet's death, his brother Claudius has taken the throne and married the widowed Queen. Hamlet is bitter that the funeral and the wedding came so close together.

questions.stem: What does the Ghost tell Hamlet in Act 1, Scene 5?
options: That Gertrude poisoned him so that she could marry his brother
That a serpent stung him as he slept in his orchard one afternoon
That Claudius poisoned his wine at a feast to celebrate a victory
That Claudius murdered him by pouring poison in his ear as he slept
questions.explanation: The official story, which the Ghost exposes as a lie, was that a serpent stung the King in his orchard. The Ghost reveals that Claudius poured poison into his ear, and orders Hamlet to take revenge but to leave Gertrude to heaven.

questions.stem: Why does Hamlet have the players perform The Murder of Gonzago?
options: To distract the court while Horatio searches the King's rooms for evidence
To prove Claudius's guilt to the whole court and so win the courtiers' support
To test the Ghost's story by watching how Claudius reacts to a similar murder
To expose Gertrude's part in the murder by watching how she reacts to it
questions.explanation: Hamlet fears the Ghost may be a devil sent to trick him. The play, which he calls the Mousetrap, copies the murder, and when Claudius rises and calls for lights, Hamlet takes it as proof. The test is private, shared only with Horatio, and aimed at the King rather than the Queen.

questions.stem: Why does Hamlet not kill Claudius when he finds him alone and praying?
options: He still doubts whether the Ghost has told him the truth
He fears that killing a king would damn his own soul
He believes killing him at prayer would send his soul to heaven
He hears guards coming and fears he will be caught in the act
questions.explanation: Hamlet wants Claudius damned, as his father died without confession. The irony is that Claudius cannot really pray: he admits his 'words fly up' while his thoughts stay below.

questions.stem: Who does Hamlet kill in his mother's room in Act 3, Scene 4?
options: Laertes, who has returned from France to defend Gertrude
Claudius, who has hidden there to spy on Hamlet and Gertrude
Polonius, who is hiding behind a tapestry to listen
Rosencrantz, who has been sent to bring him to the King
questions.explanation: Hearing a cry behind the arras, Hamlet stabs through it, hoping it is the King. It is Polonius. The killing gives Claudius a reason to send Hamlet away and makes Laertes a second avenger.

questions.stem: What does Claudius send to England with Hamlet, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern?
options: A gift of gold asking the English king to keep Hamlet at his court
A sealed letter asking the English king to imprison Hamlet for his madness
A message asking England to find Hamlet a suitable foreign bride
A sealed letter ordering the English king to have Hamlet put to death
questions.explanation: Claudius cannot kill Hamlet openly because Gertrude and the people love him. Hamlet later finds the commission, rewrites it with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern's names, and seals it with his father's signet ring.

questions.stem: What do Claudius and Laertes plan for the fencing match?
options: Laertes will use a poisoned sword, and Gertrude will hand Hamlet a poisoned cup
Laertes will use an unblunted, poisoned sword, with a poisoned drink as a backup
Laertes will lose on purpose so that Hamlet drops his guard and can be arrested
Claudius will stop the match and accuse Hamlet of trying to kill Laertes
questions.explanation: Claudius suggests an unblunted sword; Laertes adds poison to its tip; Claudius prepares a poisoned cup in case Hamlet is not hit. Their plotting turns the 'friendly' match into a trap; Gertrude knows nothing of it.

questions.stem: How does Ophelia die?
options: She dies of grief in the castle after her father's funeral
She drowns in a brook, as Gertrude reports to Laertes
She is poisoned by Claudius to stop her talking about Hamlet
She drowns herself in the sea, as Horatio reports to Claudius
questions.explanation: Gertrude describes Ophelia falling from a willow into the brook while making garlands. Because her death is 'doubtful', the priest allows her only 'maimed rites', a reduced funeral.

questions.stem: How does Gertrude die in the final scene?
options: She is wounded by the poisoned sword as she tries to stop the fight
She takes poison herself after learning the truth about Claudius
She is forced by Hamlet to drink the rest of the poisoned wine
She drinks from the poisoned cup that Claudius prepared for Hamlet
questions.explanation: Gertrude drinks to Hamlet's success despite Claudius telling her not to. 'The drink, the drink!' she cries, and her death helps expose the King's plot. It is Claudius whom Hamlet forces to drink.

questions.stem: Who is left to rule Denmark at the end of the play?
options: Fortinbras of Norway, who has Hamlet's dying support
Horatio, whom Hamlet names as the next King of Denmark
Laertes, whom the mob had cried up as king in Act 4
Rosencrantz, who returns from England in triumph
questions.explanation: Hamlet gives Fortinbras his 'dying voice'. Fortinbras, whose father lost lands to old Hamlet, gains the whole kingdom without a fight and orders a soldier's funeral for Hamlet.

questions.stem: What is Horatio's role in the play?
options: A player who speaks the lines Hamlet adds to the play
Hamlet's loyal friend, who survives to tell his story
Claudius's adviser, who spies on Hamlet for the King
Ophelia's brother, who returns to avenge his father
questions.explanation: Horatio is a fellow student from Wittenberg whom Hamlet trusts completely. When Horatio tries to drink the poison, Hamlet stops him and asks him 'To tell my story.'

questions.stem: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are best described as:
options: Gravediggers whose jokes about death make Hamlet think of Yorick
Courtiers who secretly help Hamlet escape from the ship to England
Hamlet's old school friends, who agree to spy on him for Claudius
Norwegian ambassadors who arrange peace between Denmark and Norway
questions.explanation: Claudius summons them to find out why Hamlet is acting strangely. Hamlet soon forces them to admit they were sent for, and their loyalty to the King finally costs them their lives in England.

questions.stem: How does Laertes act as a foil to Hamlet?
options: He also delays his revenge, showing that Hamlet's hesitation is natural
He goes mad from grief, showing what Hamlet might have become without Horatio
He seizes the throne by force, showing what Hamlet should have done in Act 1
He rushes to avenge his father, showing what action without thought looks like
questions.explanation: Laertes storms the palace with a mob and says he would cut Hamlet's throat in church. His speed contrasts with Hamlet's delay, but it also makes him easy for Claudius to use.

questions.stem: Hamlet, Laertes and Fortinbras have something in common that shapes the play's structure. What is it?
options: Each is a prince who has been kept from the throne by an ambitious uncle
Each has studied at Wittenberg and returns to Denmark at the King's death
Each feigns madness for a time to hide his true plans from the court
Each is a son whose father has been killed, and each responds differently
questions.explanation: Old Hamlet, Polonius and old Fortinbras all die violently. Setting three avenging sons side by side invites the audience to compare thought and action, honour and its cost.

questions.stem: What does Claudius's prayer scene in Act 3, Scene 3 add to our view of him?
options: He feels real guilt but will not give up the crown and queen he gained by murder
He truly repents of the murder, and his prayer for forgiveness is accepted by heaven
He is ready to confess publicly but is stopped by Polonius's sudden death
He regrets the murder because it has failed to win him Gertrude's love
questions.explanation: Claudius admits his offence 'smells to heaven' but cannot repent while he still enjoys its rewards. The scene makes him a more complex villain, a capable king troubled by conscience.

questions.stem: What does the play leave uncertain about Gertrude?
options: Whether she married Claudius before or after the old King died
Whether she sides with Claudius when Laertes storms in
Whether she knew that Claudius murdered her first husband
Whether the Ghost appears to her in the closet scene
questions.explanation: The Ghost condemns her remarriage but tells Hamlet to 'leave her to heaven'. Her shock in the closet scene suggests she did not know of the murder, but the play never says so outright. By contrast, she plainly sees nothing of the Ghost in that scene and holds Laertes back to protect Claudius.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Ophelia's position in the play?
options: She is Claudius's most trusted spy and freely chooses to report on Hamlet
She rejects Hamlet because his cruelty has made her stop loving him
She is protected by Gertrude, who arranges her marriage to Hamlet
She is controlled by her father and brother, and has little power over her own life
questions.explanation: Laertes and Polonius both tell her to reject Hamlet, and Polonius uses her as bait to spy on him. After her father's death she goes mad, and her songs show the grief she was never allowed to express.

questions.stem: Hamlet is a revenge tragedy. Which feature is typical of that genre?
options: A shipwreck, twins mistaken for each other, and weddings
A fool's songs, a pair of lovers, and an exile in a forest
A clever servant who fools his master to win a fortune
A ghost demanding revenge, a delay, and a bloody ending
questions.explanation: Elizabethan revenge tragedies, such as Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy, used ghosts, feigned madness, plays within plays and a stage full of bodies. Shakespeare uses the form but makes the avenger think deeply about it.

questions.stem: The Ghost says he is 'Doomed for a certain term to walk the night' and burn by day. Why might this have troubled Shakespeare's audience?
options: It proves the Ghost is a devil, which the audience would have known at once
It describes the Catholic purgatory, which Protestant England officially denied
It reflects the Protestant belief that ghosts were souls returning from purgatory
It shows the Ghost is a pagan spirit, which Elizabethan law forbade on stage
questions.explanation: Purgatory was a Catholic belief rejected by the Church of England. Its presence makes the Ghost's nature uncertain, which is why Hamlet worries the spirit 'May be a devil' and tests it.

questions.stem: Why does it matter that Hamlet has been a student at Wittenberg?
options: It shows his loyalty to the Catholic Church and its traditional teachings
It shows that Claudius has sent him away to keep him from the throne
It marks him as a thoughtful scholar, more given to reflection than action
It shows that he has trained as a soldier and is ready to lead an army
questions.explanation: Wittenberg was a famous university, linked with Martin Luther and the Protestant Reformation, and Claudius in fact refuses to let Hamlet go back there. Hamlet's education helps explain his habit of questioning and reasoning, which delays the simple act of revenge.

questions.stem: Claudius says 'There's such divinity doth hedge a king' when Laertes storms in. What belief is he drawing on?
options: That kings must be elected by the people to be accepted
That kings should share their power with a parliament
That kings are equal to their subjects in the eyes of law
That kings rule by God's will and are protected by heaven
questions.explanation: The idea of the divine right of kings made killing a king a crime against God. Coming from a man who murdered a king, the line is deeply ironic.

questions.stem: Which idea is most central to Hamlet?
options: The value of a quick and decisive military response
The corrupting power of romantic love over reason
The difficulty of acting when certainty is impossible
The rewards that come to those who obey their parents
questions.explanation: Hamlet must act on a ghost's word, in a court full of spies and lies. His delay comes from doubt, conscience and thought, and the play asks whether thinking makes action harder.

questions.stem: How does the play explore appearance and reality?
options: Characters hide their true selves behind smiles, acting and feigned madness
Characters show their true natures in public, while soliloquies conceal them
Characters disguise themselves in costume to move through the court unseen
Characters are misled by the Ghost, which turns out to be a devil in disguise
questions.explanation: Claudius smiles while guilty, Polonius and Rosencrantz spy, and Hamlet puts on an 'antic disposition'. Hamlet's first long speech rejects 'seems', yet he too must pretend.

questions.stem: Is Hamlet's madness real or feigned? Which reading is best supported by the text?
options: He feigns madness to win Ophelia's sympathy and her father's consent
He is driven mad by Ophelia's death, which is what first makes him delay
He plans to feign madness, though grief and stress at times make the line unclear
He is truly mad from his first meeting with the Ghost and merely claims to be acting
questions.explanation: Hamlet tells his friends he may 'put an antic disposition on', and he tells Rosencrantz and Guildenstern he is 'but mad north-north-west'. Yet his wild behaviour, as with Ophelia, leaves room to argue it sometimes becomes real.

questions.stem: How does Hamlet's attitude change in Act 5?
options: He comes to accept that providence shapes events and that he must be ready
He gives up revenge and decides to return to Wittenberg with Horatio
He grows more anxious and plans each step of the duel in careful detail
He decides to win the crown by persuading the people to rise against Claudius
questions.explanation: After the sea voyage Hamlet speaks of 'a divinity that shapes our ends' and says 'The readiness is all.' He no longer tries to plan everything, and he faces the duel calmly.

questions.stem: What does the graveyard scene in Act 5, Scene 1 mainly explore?
options: The gravediggers' grief for the people they have buried
The hope that the dead return to guide the living as ghosts
Death as the great leveller, which reduces everyone to dust
The way a royal funeral shows the power of the Danish crown
questions.explanation: Holding the skull of Yorick, the King's jester, Hamlet reflects that even Alexander the Great returned to dust. Death treats kings, lawyers and jesters alike.

questions.stem: What is the main dramatic purpose of Hamlet's soliloquies?
options: They let the audience hear his private thoughts, which no one on stage hears
They let Hamlet confide his plans to Horatio, his one trusted friend
They let the court learn his plans, so that Claudius can try to stop him
They let Hamlet summarise offstage events the audience has not seen
questions.explanation: Alone on stage, Hamlet reveals his grief, doubt and self-criticism. The soliloquies make the audience his confidants, so we know more than anyone at Elsinore.

questions.stem: The Mousetrap is a play within a play. What is the effect of this device?
options: It gives Ophelia a chance to declare her love for Hamlet in public
It reflects the main plot and draws attention to acting and pretending
It gives the audience a comic break that has no link to the main plot
It reveals Claudius's guilt to the whole court, who turn against him
questions.explanation: The players act out a murder like Claudius's, while the court watches and the audience watches the court. It sharpens the theme of performance in a play where many characters act a part.

questions.stem: When does the audience first hear Claudius himself admit his guilt?
options: In Act 1, Scene 2, when he tells the court why he married Gertrude so soon
In Act 5, Scene 2, when Laertes forces him to confess to the whole court
In Act 2, Scene 2, when he tells Rosencrantz and Guildenstern the truth
In an aside in Act 3, Scene 1, when Polonius's words lash his conscience
questions.explanation: Before the Mousetrap, Claudius says aside, 'How smart a lash that speech doth give my conscience!' The audience now knows the Ghost spoke truly, while Hamlet is still unsure.

questions.stem: Hamlet is full of images of disease, rot and poison. What do they suggest?
options: That Claudius's crime has corrupted the whole state of Denmark
That a plague is spreading through Elsinore and killing the court
That Hamlet's grief is a sickness he should cure by moving on
That Gertrude's guilt is slowly poisoning her body and mind
questions.explanation: From 'Something is rotten in the state of Denmark' to Claudius's admission that his crime 'smells to heaven', the imagery links one secret murder to a sick kingdom. Even the deaths at the end come by poison. Calling Hamlet's grief unhealthy is Claudius's argument in Act 1, not what the imagery suggests.

questions.stem: Why does Hamlet often speak in prose rather than verse when others are present?
options: Prose marks comic scenes that have no link to the tragic plot
Prose suits his pretended madness and his mocking, quick-witted talk
Prose shows that he is from a lower social class than the courtiers
Prose signals his deepest private feelings when he speaks alone
questions.explanation: Noble characters usually speak verse, but Hamlet slips into prose with Polonius and the courtiers as he plays the madman. His soliloquies, where he is most himself, are in verse.

questions.stem: Who says 'Frailty, thy name is woman!', and about whom?
options: Claudius, about Gertrude's grief for her son
Hamlet, about Gertrude's quick remarriage
Laertes, about Ophelia's love for Hamlet
Polonius, about his daughter's disobedience
questions.explanation: In his first soliloquy in Act 1, Scene 2, Hamlet is disgusted that his mother married Claudius so soon. He turns his anger at one woman into a judgement on all women.

questions.stem: Who says 'Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.'?
options: Hamlet, after the Ghost has told its story
Horatio, as he first sees the Ghost appear
Fortinbras, when he finds the bodies at the end
Marcellus, as Hamlet follows the Ghost
questions.explanation: Marcellus, one of the watchmen, says it in Act 1, Scene 4. The line sets up the play's imagery of corruption spreading from the crown through the country.

questions.stem: Hamlet says, 'The time is out of joint. O cursed spite, / That ever I was born to set it right!' What does this show?
options: He is eager to take the crown from his uncle
He believes the Ghost has lied to him about it
He is proud to have been chosen for the task
He sees revenge as a heavy duty he does not want
questions.explanation: Straight after the Ghost leaves in Act 1, Scene 5, Hamlet feels the world is broken and that he alone must fix it. He resents the burden from the start, which helps explain his delay.

questions.stem: What does Hamlet mean by 'The play's the thing / Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the King.'?
options: He will write a play to win back Ophelia's love
He will act in a play to hide from Claudius's spies
He will stage a play to persuade the court to rebel
He will use a play to reveal Claudius's guilt
questions.explanation: At the end of Act 2, Hamlet decides to test the Ghost's word. Drama itself becomes the means of discovering the truth.

questions.stem: Claudius says, 'My words fly up, my thoughts remain below. / Words without thoughts never to heaven go.' What does he realise?
options: His prayer has been heard, so Hamlet cannot harm him
His plan to send Hamlet to England is sure to work
His prayer is empty because he will not truly repent
His words have convinced the court that he is innocent
questions.explanation: He says this at the end of Act 3, Scene 3, just after Hamlet has spared him for being at prayer. The irony is sharp: Hamlet held back for a prayer that never reached heaven.

questions.stem: In Act 5, Scene 2, Hamlet tells Horatio, 'The readiness is all.' What does the line show?
options: A plan to strike Claudius the moment the duel begins
A fear that he has not practised enough to beat Laertes
A wish to delay revenge until he is sure of the Ghost
A calm acceptance of whatever fate brings, including death
questions.explanation: Before the duel, Horatio offers to call it off, and Hamlet refuses. 'If it be now, 'tis not to come': he trusts providence instead of plotting, a change from his earlier agonised thinking.

questions.stem: For the question 'To what extent is Hamlet a play about the paralysing effects of thought?', which is the strongest thesis?
options: Shakespeare shows that Hamlet's thinking delays revenge, though doubt about the Ghost also justifies it
Hamlet is a play by William Shakespeare in which Prince Hamlet must avenge his murdered father
This essay will explore whether Hamlet thinks too much in the play written by William Shakespeare
In Hamlet there are many soliloquies, and Hamlet speaks most of them while alone on the stage
questions.explanation: A strong thesis answers the question directly and shows the extent, here 'though'. The others retell, announce or describe without arguing.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Hamlet holds Yorick's skull and talks about him.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: List the other skulls that the gravedigger throws up out of the grave
Describe the rest of the graveyard scene in order, line by line
Explain how the skull makes Hamlet face death as the end that awaits everyone
Add how long Yorick had been dead and what his job was at the old King's court
questions.explanation: Analysis says what the evidence suggests. Linking the skull to Hamlet's new acceptance of death connects the moment to the play's ideas about mortality and readiness.
